title: Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38)
hook: shown his own seal, Judah says "She is more righteous than I"

segments.voice: Yesterday, into the pit: Joseph sold, and Reuben back too late. Your line was don't come back too late. Did the good thing get done? Today the Torah steps away from Joseph, and follows Judah, the brother who said sell him. Day sixty-seven.

Right in the middle of Joseph's story, just as he's dragged off to Egypt, the Torah cuts away. It's like a TV show that suddenly spends a whole episode on a side character. And the side character is Judah. Judah has sons. The oldest marries a woman named Tamar, and dies. By the custom of the time, the next son should give her a child in his brother's name. He refuses, and dies too. Judah has one son left, and he's afraid. So he sends Tamar back to her father's house: wait until my youngest grows up. And then he never sends for her. Tamar is left waiting, a widow with no future. Today: what she does about it.
screen: `THE STORY CUTS AWAY TO JUDAH.` → `TAMAR, TWICE A WIDOW.` → `SENT HOME TO WAIT, AND FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Years pass. Tamar hears that Judah is coming through on the way to shear his sheep. She takes off her widow's clothes, covers her face with a veil, and sits by the road. Judah doesn't recognize her. He thinks she's a woman for hire. He has nothing to pay with, so she asks for a pledge: your seal, your cord, and your staff. His ID card, basically. He hands them over. Three months later, word comes: Tamar is pregnant. Judah, the head of the family, gives the sentence: bring her out and let her be burned. And as she's being brought out, Tamar sends a message. Not an accusation. She doesn't say, it was you. She sends the seal, the cord and the staff, and says: the man who owns these is the father. Please look, whose are these? That word, look, recognize, is the same Hebrew the brothers used when they handed Jacob the bloody coat and said, look, is this your son's? Judah once asked his father to recognize something, as a lie. Now he's asked to recognize something true. And he does. "She is more righteous than I." The Talmud notices how Tamar did it. She was ready to die rather than shame him in public. She gave him the chance to admit it himself. And he did, in front of everyone. Tamar has twins, Perez and Zerah. And from Perez, the book of Ruth tells us, comes King David.
screen: `TAMAR WAITS BY THE ROAD.` · `A SEAL, A CORD, A STAFF.` · `WHOSE ARE THESE? LOOK.` · `SHE IS MORE RIGHTEOUS THAN I.` · then, large: `FROM PEREZ, KING DAVID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one time someone else was right. Settle, and breathe. Think of a disagreement, big or small, where you dug in, and later realized the other person had it right. Maybe you never told them. Picture saying Judah's words in your own way: you were right, and I was wrong. Notice what that feels like in your chest. Heavy? Lighter? If there's someone you can tell today, you might. The bell holds the time.
Judah and Tamar. She was wronged and left waiting; he judged her, then recognized his own seal and said she was the righteous one.
Your line: she was right. Today, when someone turns out to be right, say so out loud, even if it costs you a little. Day sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition draws from Tamar the teaching that publicly shaming another person is gravely wrong, and honors Judah's admission as a model of owning a mistake; Tamar's son Perez is remembered as an ancestor of King David.

fork.setup: you're Tamar, being led out to be burned. you hold the proof of who the father is: Judah's own seal, cord and staff. what do you do?
options: shout his name in front of everyone.
send him the items privately and let him decide.
stay silent and accept the sentence.
fork.reveal: she sends the items with a quiet question, whose are these? the Talmud says she'd rather die than shame him. Judah admits it: she is more righteous than I.

original.note: Hebrew: please recognize, look. said to Jacob about the coat, and to Judah about his seal.

trapdoor: what you thought: an odd side story dropped into Joseph's.
what it means: the brother who sold Joseph learns to say I was wrong, and that change matters later.
what a scholar hears: haker na links 37:32 and 38:25 (Genesis Rabbah 84–85 notices it). Sotah 10b draws the rule about public shame from Tamar.

Levirate custom (yibbum) summarized as 'give her a child in his brother's name'; Onan's refusal summarized. Confirm.
haker na link between 37:32 and 38:25: Genesis Rabbah 84:19 / 85:11. Confirm citation.
